reasoning.Student A:
I will report my true preferences because, under the standard student-proposing deferred acceptance (DA) mechanism used in many school-choice settings, it is a dominant strategy for students to rank schools truthfully. Misrepresenting preferences cannot yield a strictly better outcome and can only risk a worse one.

Concretely for my situation:
- My sincere ranking is x > y > w > z.
- I have high priority (rank 1) at w and y and lower priority (rank 2) at x and z.
- Many other applicants favor y > x > w > z, so y will be competitive. However, since I prefer x to y I should still list x first; if I am displaced at x I have good fallback at y because I have top priority there.
- Listing a less-preferred school ahead of a more-preferred one (to try to “game” priorities) is unnecessary and risky because DA is strategy-proof for students.

Therefore I will submit the complete ranking in my sincere order.

Assuming the matching uses the standard student-proposing deferred acceptance algorithm (the usual school-choice mechanism), it is strategy-proof for students: you cannot improve your outcome by misreporting preferences. So you should rank schools in true preference order.

Relevant facts: my true preferences are w > x > y > z. My priorities are lower (2) at w and y and higher (1) at x and z. Many other applicants favor y > x > w > z, so y will be highly contested; that makes getting y uncertain for me (priority 2). That might tempt me to list x ahead of w to lock in a school where I have top priority, but under DA that is unnecessary and can only harm me. Listing my true order maximizes my chance of getting the best feasible school given others' choices and priorities.

Therefore I will submit my sincere ranking: w > x > y > z.
